questions.stem: A teammate asks why the team should use version control for documentation. What is the best answer?
questions.explanation: Version control tracks history and supports safe collaboration, even for documentation.

options.text: It records changes and helps people collaborate without overwriting each other.
options.explanation: Version control keeps a history of documentation edits and supports coordinated work across contributors.
Visibility is controlled separately.

options.text: It removes the need to review content.
options.explanation: Review is still important.

options.text: It prevents anyone from editing files locally.
options.explanation: Git supports local editing.

questions.stem: Order the steps to create a reviewed README update in a repository.
questions.explanation: A branch isolates the change, a PR reviews it, and merge updates main.

explanations.s1: Starting from main on a new branch keeps the README update isolated.
explanations.s2: The README is edited on that branch so main remains unchanged during review.
explanations.s3: A pull request presents the README diff for comments and checks.
explanations.s4: After review, merging brings the accepted README update into the target branch.

questions.stem: Order the pull request feedback loop before a GitHub flow change is merged.
questions.explanation: After reviewers request changes, the author updates the same branch, requests another look, waits for approval or passing requirements, and then merges.

items.text: Push review fixes to the same branch
Ask reviewers to re-check the pull request
Wait for approval or required checks to pass

explanations.s1: Follow-up commits on the same branch update the open pull request automatically.
explanations.s2: Requesting another review signals that the feedback has been addressed.
explanations.s3: Approval or required checks should be satisfied before the change is accepted.
explanations.s4: The merge happens after the reviewed pull request is ready.
